body.heading: Why atoms team up
paragraphs: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds. Atoms bond because of their electrons: by sharing electrons, or handing them over, atoms can reach more stable arrangements than they manage alone. A lone hydrogen atom is restless and reactive; two of them sharing electrons settle down as a calm hydrogen molecule.

A molecule can be built from a single element — the oxygen in the air is O₂, pairs of oxygen atoms — or from several, in which case it is also a compound. Water, H₂O, is both a molecule and a compound: two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

body.heading: Formulas, shapes and sizes
paragraphs: Chemists write a molecule as a formula that counts its atoms: CO₂ is one carbon and two oxygens, and glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is a team of 24 atoms. The count matters, because changing it changes the substance — add one oxygen atom to CO and the poisonous carbon monoxide becomes the carbon dioxide you breathe out.

Molecules also have shapes, and shape matters as much as the ingredient list. Water molecules are bent, which is part of why water behaves so unusually, and the molecules in your nose are shape-detectors: they respond to the outlines of scent molecules, which is how smell works.

body.heading: From two atoms to two metres
paragraphs: Most familiar molecules are small, but nothing limits their size. A single drop of water holds well over a thousand billion billion molecules, yet at the other extreme, one DNA molecule from a single human cell would stretch about two metres if it were carefully unravelled — all of it packed into a nucleus far too small to see.
Plastics, proteins and starches are molecules too, built as long chains of repeating units. Chemistry's teams range from a pair of atoms holding on to each other to chains of millions.

description: When atoms join together they form molecules — from the oxygen you breathe to the long chains of atoms that make up your DNA.
